AI: only 40% of companies rate their ROI as very good

Companies are investing heavily in artificial intelligence. But are they really getting value from it? A survey of US e-commerce companies conducted in May 2025, included in Statista's dossier on AI in US e-commerce, gives a nuanced answer.

About 40% of companies surveyed (39% to be precise) rated the return on investment of AI as very good. That is far from a failure: 56% rated it good. But only a minority feel they are getting the full benefit, and that says something about how AI is being deployed.

What the numbers say

The full breakdown is as follows: 39% of companies rate the ROI of AI as very good, 56% as good, 2% as poor and 2% are not sure. In total, 95% of companies surveyed therefore see a positive return.

Yet the most interesting figure is the gap between "good" and "very good". For most companies, AI brings a gain, but not the step change hoped for at the time of the investment. It improves things without transforming them.

Understanding what sets the 39% apart is therefore more useful than asking whether AI "works" in general.

Adoption is still young

Part of the explanation is maturity. The same dossier shows that in 2024, 47% of consumer goods and retail companies were still in pilot mode with generative AI. 20% were in early production, and only 5% used it fully across the organization.

A technology still being tested rarely pays off as much as one built into processes. Many companies are still looking for where AI can really make a difference, running trials on a wide range of topics.

Experimentation has its place, but it needs to lead somewhere measurable.

Returns come from targeted uses

The AI projects that pay off most often share three traits. They address a precise, measurable problem. They rely on data the company already has. And their results can be used directly by business teams.

Customer feedback analysis ticks all three boxes. The problem is clear: understanding why customers are unhappy or leave. The data already exists: reviews, tickets, emails, calls. And the results immediately serve customer service, marketing and product teams.

By contrast, AI projects that are too broad, without their own data or a measurable goal, struggle more to prove their value.

These projects also have the advantage of being understood by everyone: a customer service manager immediately grasps what "30% of complaints are about delivery times" means.

That clarity makes it easier to decide what to fix, and to show the result a few weeks later.

A market that confirms the interest

The market for automatic language analysis, which covers this kind of use, illustrates the trend. According to Statista Market Insights, it was worth $126.05 billion in 2025 and could reach $868.73 billion by 2032.

We covered that trajectory in detail in our article on the growth of the language analysis market. It shows that companies see automatic understanding of texts and conversations as a high-value use.

How to join the 40%

To get a very good return, it is better to start small and concrete. Pick an existing data source, such as customer reviews or support tickets. Define a precise question: what are the three main reasons for dissatisfaction? Then measure the effect of the fixes you make.

This kind of project delivers results within weeks, without a dedicated technical team. The analysis relies on models such as Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case, chosen for the need rather than the trend.

And when the data concerns customers, where it is hosted matters: at custovox.ai, it stays in France and is never used to train models.

The takeaway

AI pays off for almost every company surveyed, but it pays off a lot for only a minority. The difference has less to do with the technology than with the choice of use. The most profitable projects rely on data you already have and answer a clear business question.

Conversations with your customers are probably the richest and least used source of data in your company.

Start there, measure, and expand once the first results are in.
